name: Cinsault

lines.s10: Cinsault is the pale, perfumed red of the Mediterranean: wild strawberry, raspberry and rose petal, soft enough to serve cool.
lines.s20: Cinsault is a grape of the hot south of France, at ease in heat and drought. It gives pale, soft wines of strawberry and raspberry, and it is the quiet partner in many Provence rosés and southern French reds.
lines.s45: Cinsault has spent most of its life in other grapes' company, softening the red blends and filling the rosés of southern France. On its own it is pale and perfumed, with wild strawberry, raspberry and rose petal, light in body and gentle in tannin. It is rarely given new oak. France mostly blends it or presses it for rosé, while South Africa and Chile now bottle old vines alone as light, fragrant reds. Pour it cool with charcuterie, grilled tuna or a tomato salad. Chile planted it in its southern hills after the earthquake of 1939, and those vines, now old, are bottled alone at last.
lines.sale: Cinsault is a grape behind the pale Provence rosé you already know, and as a red it keeps that same strawberry freshness. I would chill it lightly and pour it with grilled tuna or the charcuterie.

glass.lead: Wild strawberry, raspberry and red cherry with rose petal and a hint of thyme, pale, light and soft on the tongue.

ladder.where: The granite hills of Itata, near the coast of southern Chile
The Languedoc, Provence, the southern Rhône, the Swartland and the Bekaa

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity medium, tannin low and soft, alcohol medium, body light to medium; pale in colour.

old.where: The Languedoc, Provence and the southern Rhône; Lebanon's Bekaa Valley
old.glass: Usually met in a blend or as rosé: pale pink, with strawberry, red cherry and a dry, fresh finish. As a red it tends to be soft and light, with a scent of thyme.
old.cellar: Mostly blended with Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre or Carignan, or pressed early for rosé; fermented in tank, with little or no new oak.

new.where: South Africa's Swartland and Stellenbosch; Itata in southern Chile
new.glass: Typically bottled alone as a pale, fragrant red: raspberry, wild strawberry and rose petal, bright and light, with modest alcohol and fine, gentle tannin. Old vines tend to add depth without weight.
new.cellar: Old, unirrigated bush vines, often picked early; whole bunches fermented in concrete, old casks or clay jars, with no new oak, and bottled young.

contrast.why: In France it was planted to soften blends and make rosé, and the label names a place. South Africa and Chile inherited old, dry farmed vines, which growers now bottle alone under the grape's name.
contrast.blur: The Languedoc now bottles old vine Cinsault alone too, light and chilled, and South Africa still blends much of it into fuller reds with Syrah and Grenache.
contrast.call: A dry, pale rosé or a thyme scented blend leans France; a pale, perfumed red bottled alone leans the Cape or Chile.

service.temp: 54 to 59 degrees Fahrenheit, 12 to 15 degrees Celsius, as a red; colder still as a rosé.
service.glass: A Burgundy bowl for the perfume of a red bottled alone; a white wine glass for rosé.
service.decant: Usually unnecessary for a light, aromatic red.
service.age: Young, within three or four years; a few old vine reds reward five or more.

with.why: soft tannin and fresh fruit against salt and fat
a light red with little tannin to fight the fish
soft fruit suits ripe tomato and olive oil

with.dish: Mezze with grilled aubergine and lamb
with.why: the table of the Bekaa, perfume meeting smoke
a dry, cold rosé cools the mustard and cayenne

labels.means: The same grape spelt without the L, as French officials and many Cape labels write it.
The appellation of most Provence rosé, pale and dry, in which Cinsault often joins Grenache.
The Cape's old name for Cinsault, no kin to the Rhône hill; it gave Pinotage its ending.
A Chilean label term kept for dry farmed País and Cinsault from the southern coastal hills.

guest.q: I only know Cinsault from rosé. What is it like as a red?
guest.a: Much the same in spirit: pale, light and fragrant, with wild strawberry and very little tannin. Drink it as you would a rosé, lightly chilled.

guest.q: Why is this red so pale? Is something wrong with it?
guest.a: Nothing at all. Cinsault has large, juicy berries, so there is more juice to each skin and less colour and tannin to draw out. The pale colour is the grape.

guest.q: The label says old vines. Does that matter?
guest.a: With this grape it does. Young, heavily cropped Cinsault can be thin. Old vines grown without irrigation give far fewer grapes, and the wine has more scent and depth for it.

compare.tell: Grenache is fuller and warmer in alcohol, with kirsch, raspberry jam and white pepper; Cinsault is paler still, lighter and fresher, with less alcohol and more perfume.
Pinot Noir has brighter acidity, a longer finish and forest floor beneath its cherry; Cinsault is softer and simpler, with strawberry and a warmer, thyme scented feel.
Gamay is tarter, with high acidity and often banana from whole bunch fermentation; Cinsault is softer, lower in acidity and warmer in feel.

profile.st: Pale ruby · Body light to medium · Acid medium · Tannin low and soft · Alcohol medium
profile.fruit: Wild strawberry, raspberry, red cherry, redcurrant; riper strawberry in the heat of the Midi
profile.other: Rose petal, violet, thyme and black tea; little or no new oak; often blended, or pressed early for pale, dry rosé
profile.tell: Pale and perfumed, strawberry and rose petal on soft tannin and modest acidity: light as Pinot Noir, but warmer and simpler
profile.regions: The Languedoc, Provence and the southern Rhône; Lebanon's Bekaa; South Africa's Swartland and Stellenbosch; Itata in Chile; Puglia as Ottavianello
profile.confuse: Grenache is fuller and higher in alcohol; Pinot Noir has brighter acidity and forest floor; Gamay is tarter, often with banana

cards.front: Cinsault: what was it called at the Cape, and what was bred from it?
cards.back: Hermitage. In 1925 it was crossed with Pinot Noir at Stellenbosch to give Pinotage, whose name joins the two.

cards.front: Cinsault on a list: Old World or New World, what tips it?
cards.back: A dry, pale rosé or a thyme scented blend leans France. A pale, perfumed red bottled alone from old bush vines leans South Africa or Itata in Chile.

cards.front: Cinsault: when did Chile plant it, and where?
cards.back: Just after the Chillán earthquake of 1939, in the dry farmed southern hills around Itata. The label term Secano Interior is kept for it and for País.

questions.q: Two pale wines of Cinsault are poured. One is a dry rosé blended with Grenache; the other is a perfumed, lightly chilled red from old bush vines, labelled with the grape alone. Which pair of origins is the more typical, in that order?
questions.exp: A Grenache and Cinsault rosé is the classic of Provence, and old bush vine Cinsault bottled alone belongs to the Swartland's revival. The reversed pair, the nearest wrong answer, swaps the two traditions.

questions.q: A guest sees Hermitage on an old South African label and expects the grape of the Rhône hill. Which grape did the Cape mean by that name?
questions.exp: At the Cape, Hermitage was the old name for Cinsault, which is why its crossing with Pinot Noir was named Pinotage. Syrah, the nearest wrong answer, is the grape of the Rhône hill.

questions.q: A guest asks for a red to drink cool with grilled tuna, with as little tannin as the list allows. The list offers four grapes of the south of France. Which do you pour?
questions.exp: Cinsault's large, juicy berries give a pale, soft red with little tannin, which takes a chill and suits fish. Carignan, Syrah and Mourvèdre are darker and firmer, and turn hard when cold.

report: Mode contrast, as the plan fixes it. The honest difference here is less of climate than of use: France blends the grape or presses it for rosé and names a place, while South Africa and Chile bottle old vines alone under the grape's name. So why speaks of tradition, old vines and the label, and call is a tell of style and label more than of a blind glass. A reviewer who wants a stricter blind tell may prefer home and abroad.

A thin grape: the profile is written new and agrees with the Régionale row (warm to hot, acidity medium, body and tannin light, red berries and a floral scent, a blender often used for rosé, a parent of Pinotage).

The named floral and herbal notes (rose petal, violet, thyme, black tea) are a taster's naming of what the Régionale row calls floral; they stand on trade tasting notes and not on a wine body's page. A checker should weigh them.

Chile: planted in the southern hills just after the Chillán earthquake of 1939 stands on two trade sources (one says 1939, one says officially in 1940). The cellar line for the New World follows the Codex's own Itata reading (whole bunch or carbonic ferments, no new oak, concrete, old barrels or clay jars, early bottling).
Lebanon is placed in the Old World, as the brief's Mediterranean rim; the Codex's Lebanon reading calls Cinsault the Bekaa's old vine.

Left out for want of a firm second source or of room: the vineyard at Lodi in California planted in 1886 and said to hold the oldest vines of the grape, the old California name Black Malvoisie, the Jesuit planting in the Bekaa in 1857 from Algerian cuttings, and the label name Ottavianello of Puglia, which the profile's regions keep.

The label line Cinsaut says French officials and many Cape labels write it so; the national wine body of South Africa lists the grape under that spelling. The plan carries no alias for it, though the Codex's own alias list pairs Cinsault with Cinsaut: the integrator may wish to add it.
The Creole dish is shrimp remoulade with a rosé, which is how most guests meet the grape.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the sites directly. The checker should open the four addresses.

checked.verdict: Sound after five fixes. Hermitage, Cinsaut, Ottavianello, the planting in Chile after the Chillán earthquake of 1939, Secano Interior for País and Cinsault and the Bekaa hold; the guest answer and one explanation gave the grape thin skins where the sources give it fairly thick, firm ones, and the worlds question admitted a second key.
changed: guest[1].a: big berries and thin skins now reads large, juicy berries, so there is more juice to each skin. An encyclopedia and the United States germplasm record give large berries with fairly thick, firm skins; the pale colour comes from the share of juice to skin.
lines.s20: keeps its freshness in the heat now reads at ease in heat and drought. Drought resistance is in every source read; freshness in the heat is in none.

labels, Côtes de Provence: a pale, dry rosé now reads the appellation of most Provence rosé, pale and dry. It is an appellation, red and white as well, and the Codex Provence record calls it the largest.
questions[0]: the stem now asks for the more typical pair. The blur line itself admits Languedoc Cinsault bottled alone and Cape rosé, so Stellenbosch, then the Languedoc could be defended.
open: Chile: the planting is dated 1939 by most sources and officially 1940 by one; the entry says just after the earthquake of 1939.
Secano Interior as a term reserved for País and Cinsault stands on the Codex Chile record, which cites the decree; no page read in this session confirms or refutes it.
The Cinsaut alias the author raised is the plan reviewer to decide; nothing here changes it.
